title: Physics-based logarithmic description of electrostatic field enhancement in hemisphere-on-cylindrical-post structures for high-field applications
authors: Thiago A. de Assis, Fernando F. Dall-Agnol, Richard G. Forbes
abstract: Electrostatic (ES) field enhancement at sharp conducting structures plays a central role in lightning protection, corona discharge, electrical breakdown in vacuum (for example in particle accelerators), and more generally in technological applications of field electron emitters. A canonical geometry for studying this ES effect is the hemisphere-on-cylindrical-post (HCP) model, in the regime where the structure stands on a planar conductor of large lateral extent, and a large gap exists between the structure and the counter-electrode. A parameter of major interest is the apex field enhancement factor (AFEF) (apex-ES-field/background-ES-field). For this (and other) structures, a formula for the AFEF can be written in the form AFEF = ASC x ASR, where the apex sharpness ratio (ASR) is given by the ratio (post-height/apex-radius-of-curvature), and the apex sharpness coefficient (ASC) depends on the post shape. For the HCP model, no exact analytical formulas for the ASC or the AFEF are currently known. (Quite possibly none exist.) This paper develops a compact analytical approximation for the ASC and hence for the AFEF. This compact formula has a logarithmic-style structure, rather than the power-style structure used in previous approximations. When compared with precise finite-element analyses of the HCP model, over the computationally accessible range 1 to 1000 for the ASR, this logarithmic-style formula has a maximum error-magnitude of 0.15 percent, which is significantly better than older approximations.
summary: This paper presents a new, highly accurate analytical approximation for the electrostatic field enhancement factor in the hemisphere-on-cylindrical-post (HCP) structure. By deriving a compact formula with a logarithmic structure, the authors significantly improve upon previous power-law approximations. This advancement is crucial for engineering applications requiring precise knowledge of high-field regions, such as lightning protection and particle accelerator design.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of accurately modeling the electrostatic (ES) field enhancement factor (FEF) at the apex of sharp conducting structures.
main_result: The authors developed a new, compact analytical approximation for the FEF that has a logarithmic structure, achieving a maximum error of only 0.15% when compared to finite-element simulations.
method: The methodology involves deriving a new analytical formula for the apex sharpness coefficient, contrasting with older power-law approximations, and validating it against high-precision numerical simulations.
model_or_system: The canonical geometry studied is the hemisphere-on-cylindrical-post (HCP) model, which is relevant for applications like lightning protection and electrical breakdown in vacuum.
key_observables: Apex field enhancement factor ($\gamma_a$), defined as the ratio of the local ES field at the apex to the background ES field.
important_parameters: Apex sharpness ratio ($\sigma_a = h/r_a$), which characterizes the geometry of the post.
main_assumptions: The analysis focuses on the negative-field situation, and the derived formula is validated for the range $1 \le \sigma_a \le 1000$.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the axisymmetric finite-element simulation domain for the HCP model. Figure 2 compares the calculated coefficient $c_a(\sigma_a)$ against FEM results and the new analytical fit. Figure 3 compares the new formula against older, less accurate power-type fitting formulas.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical problem and the HCP model, develops the new logarithmic analytical approximation for the field enhancement factor, validates this formula against detailed finite-element simulations, and compares its accuracy against historical approximations.
why_interesting: While the physics is classical electrostatics, the rigorous mathematical development of a highly accurate, non-trivial analytical approximation (logarithmic form) for a complex physical system's limiting behavior is mathematically interesting.

Blue circles represent high-precision finite-element results obtained using the MDD technique, with an estimated relative numerical uncertainty in γa of order 10−5 %. The numerical data show a smooth and monotonic decrease of ca from the exact hemispherical value ca(1) = 3 toward a regime of progressively weaker variation as σa increases.
